text: Over $\mathbb{C}$, ___'s theorem guarantees that every finite-dimensional representation of a solvable Lie algebra has a common (simultaneous) eigenvector.
explanation: This is Lie's theorem: over $\mathbb{C}$, solvability forces a simultaneous eigenvector and hence simultaneous upper-triangularization. Contrast Engel's theorem (nilpotency, from all $\mathrm{ad}(X)$ nilpotent) and Cartan's solvability criterion (about the Killing form); here the hypothesis is solvable and the conclusion is a shared eigenvector.
